newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Sydney Olympics construction costs seen higher.
newsitem.headline: Sydney Olympics construction costs seen higher.

text.p: The forecast cost of constructing facilities for the Sydney 2000 Olympics has risen by A$124 million to A$2.1 billion, New South Wales state treasurer Michael Egan said on Tuesday.

The total cost for the Olympic Coordination Authority (OCA), the state government authority charged with building Olympic infrastructure, now stands at A$2.112 billion compared to the $1.987 billion forecast in the previous financial year.
The new figure also represents an increase of over A$500 million from the original Olympics construction budget of A$1.54 billion.
The total cost of constructing Olympic facilities and related infrastructure now stands at $3.2 billion, of which $1.1 billion is to be provided by the private sector.
Over three-quarters of the remaining $2.1 billion will be paid directly by taxpayers. Games organisers SOCOG, the federal government and other sources would provide $513 million.
Egan said A$628.1 million would be spent in the 1997/98 financial year, the biggest single slice spent in one year since Sydney won the right to host the Games in 1993.
"This is the budget that will break the back of Olympic construction expenditure," Egan said.
"All of the Olympic construction costs are being paid for now, upfront. Not a cent will be left owing by September 2000," Egan said.
The OCA budget did not include the building of the Olympic village or stadium, expected to be met by private investment.
Egan said two-thirds of the total construction budget would have been spent by the end of June 1998, with $804 million spent up to the end of the 1996-97 financial year.

The three biggest factors responsible for the 1997/98 increase were a $57 million contribution to the athlete's village, $50 million for media and technical officials' villages and $16 million for a softball venue, spokesman for Olympics minister and SOCOG president Michael Knight said.
Of the $628 million to be spent in 1997/98, $362 million would be paid by New South Wales and the rest would be met by SOCOG and federal government grants.
This compares to a net cost of $404 million to the state in the previous financial year, Knight's spokesman said.
The private sector would spend over $300 million on the Olympic stadium and village in the coming financial year, meaning about $2.5 million would be spent a day on Olympic construction projects.

Of the $628 million to be spent in 1997/98, $179 million has been set aside for the completion of the new Sydney Showground at the Olympic site and relocation of the annual Royal Easter Show to Homebush.
Another $147.8 million would be spent on roads and related projects, $52.7 million on site remediation and $34.8 million as the government's contribution to the Olympic stadium.
SOCOG's budget, to be announced on Wednesday, has also risen. Knight said last month it had grown to $2.4 billion from an original estimate of $1.7 billion.

State opposition leader Peter Collins last month introduced proposed legislation aimed at forcing the government to make regular reports on the cost of the Games, including expenditure reviews and estimates of future costs.
A major factor in Sydney winning the Olympic bid was that the state government would underwrite the cost of the Games.
The controversial Atlanta Olympics last year were not government-backed and Games organisers forced to cover a US$1.7 billion budget struggled to break even.
